text: User corrected single-source verification of current events - multiple sources should be checked before reporting on news/political figures
User uses 'sorry continue' to resume after interruptions, expecting the assistant to pick up exactly where it left off

IIFE / scope-wrappers in JSX are a recurring smell the agent introduces; before adding any inline wrapper in JSX, check surrounding siblings for the prevailing pattern (inline prop or plain const) and conform to it.

Silently zero-defaulting missing fields in structured data (e.g., bounding-box coordinates defaulting to 0) produces fabricated downstream values that look valid; missing or partial data must be explicitly flagged rather than filled with silent defaults.

A terse 'keep going' continuation message after a frustrating turn does not grant license to advance to the next planned scope or phase; it resumes the current task only and carries the affect of the prior turn.

The user strongly prefers auto-generated or derived indices over hand-maintained ones; where a file has both policy and census sections, a marker-based split (e.g., '<!-- AUTO-GENERATED BELOW -->') lets the hand-written portion stay stable while the generated portion refreshes cleanly.

When formalizing a repeated manual workflow loop into a skill, implement the logic as testable shell scripts first and have SKILL.md call those scripts — this keeps the skill prompt readable and makes the logic independently verifiable.

Spawning a dedicated adversarial sub-agent (validator or skeptical-reviewer role) before declaring complex multi-phase work done consistently surfaces real blockers that the implementing agent missed; treat the adversarial pass as a required step, not an optional sanity check.

Framing each fix batch as 'this will fix it' or 'this addresses the gap' when the prior ship also made that claim and failed is a sycophantic pattern that erodes trust; if structural gaps have recurred, say so explicitly and describe the structural change, not just the additive fix.

High-cost agent modes (full multi-agent runs, expensive fan-outs) should default to a cheaper tier and require explicit user confirmation before escalating — surprising the user with a costly run when a lite mode would have sufficed breaks trust on cost.

When a user's repeated manual workflow becomes the de facto development loop across multiple sessions, that loop is a strong signal to formalize it as a named skill rather than re-establishing it from scratch each session.

When proposing a new storage backend (e.g., Redis) for a feature when an existing store (e.g., Mongo) is already in use, proactively justify the new dependency rather than waiting for the user to push back — the default should be 'use what's already there unless there's a concrete reason not to'.
Animation/visual enhancement code was added as an unsolicited 'enhancement' and was flagged as incorrect/unwanted - adding unrequested visual effects to UI code is a mistake
User runs very large tool-call sessions (50-150+ tools) for complex feature work, suggesting tolerance for long autonomous execution when given clear direction ('started with them', 'keep going')
High tool-use sessions (50-157 tools) are common for continuation and complex implementation tasks; this is normal and expected for this project

When designing inter-agent messaging for inactive sessions, the correct pattern is inbox persistence so a resuming agent can discover queued messages — do not attempt to resurrect or re-awaken dead sessions to deliver messages
When restructuring or standardizing existing documentation, preserve [VERIFY] and TODO(human) markers exactly in place — do not remove, resolve, or rewrite them unless the user explicitly directs it

When asked to plan multi-phase work, each step should include its intent, concrete validation criteria, and failure-detection signals, then be codified into a persistent reference document the system can use for future validation

System-supplied date values can drift across turns within a single session; documents created in later turns may receive different dates than earlier ones — re-read the current date rather than reusing one captured at session start

Building a UI that looks structurally correct (tabs, config sections, renders) but reads as a form viewer rather than an interactive tool means the user's intent — live customization with immediate feedback — was not modeled; implement the intent, not the structural shape
The agent must not declare code 'ready' or 'done' and allow it to be committed/pushed when it contains a known pattern violation that has already been corrected in prior sessions.
When the agent declares a test or feature 'successful', it must show actual output for the user to inspect rather than asserting success without evidence.

When the user explicitly invokes a mandatory skill like /atone, the agent must not skip or defer it — skipping a correction ritual while in the middle of being corrected is a compounding failure that erodes trust.

When a caching strategy invalidates a shared tag (e.g. `revalidateTag`), the agent must proactively surface the blast radius: one user's event invalidating cache state for all users is a critical design flaw that must be caught before implementation, not after.

When a report or doc introduces a named constant or config value (e.g. WORKER_MAX_DEFER_COUNT), it must define and explain what that value does inline; naming a config without explaining it forces the reader to hunt for meaning.

Before asking for permission to run a mutating command against an external service (render, vercel, cloud infra), show the exact command and a plain-English description of its effect; never prompt first and explain second.

Invoking /atone without completing the full event-recording flow (gathering context, picking a slug, running atone.sh add) leaves the mistake unrecorded and triggers a stop-hook gate on the next turn; the invocation and the recording must happen in the same turn.
Multi-agent task orchestration generates large volumes of task notification events; most are silently acknowledged without substantive processing
When user instructs 'commit and push', proceed directly without showing diffs or prompting for confirmation — user expects silent execution
User uses /core-dump proactively at session milestones and before exit, not just at end — treat it as a mid-session tool too
Sessions with many continuations (high 'this session being continued from' frequency) indicate context compaction happening often — proactive checkpointing reduces recovery overhead

When a circuit breaker or rate-limiting mechanism is scoped to a shared resource rather than a per-module or per-pipeline-step key, the agent must proactively flag that a failure in one consumer will block all other consumers — even those using different logic on the same dependency.

Silent zero-defaults in data extraction (e.g. `bb.get('x', 0)`) fabricate plausible-looking numeric values when source data is missing or partial, producing downstream motion/delta claims that are entirely fabricated rather than absent.

The agent should never commit or push for protected projects (those in an explicit protected-repos registry); it must prepare the change, show the diff, and hand the commit to the user. Authorization to commit elsewhere does not extend to protected repos.
When a user says a behavior is 'too noisy' or 'too aggressive', the correct response is to tune it down, not turn it off entirely — the complaint is a ceiling on intensity, not a removal mandate.
User reassurance ('I trust you', 'that's fine') is not authorization to remove safeguards, gates, or confirmations — it is social comfort, not a blanket removal mandate.

When a task list has not been updated across many turns but significant editing has occurred, the list has drifted from reality and must be reconciled before stopping — completed work marked done, new work added, in-progress set correctly.

When a feature unexpectedly requires adding a new library or dependency, the agent should surface this constraint to the user and offer a within-existing-dependency alternative first rather than proceeding with the addition.

One-off inline styling for a UI element (instead of reusing the existing component hover/interactive patterns) is a signal that there is a gap in the UI kit — surface this observation rather than writing one-off CSS.

Runtime dogfooding and live exercise catch bugs that a large test suite (99+ tests) misses; claimed correctness from test coverage alone is insufficient — actually running the affected path is a separate, necessary gate.

Config tools that perform validation only at parse time (not at write time) can silently break unrelated features when a required field is missing; always verify the full config profile loads correctly after editing, not just the targeted field.

A task list that accumulates many edits without corresponding TaskUpdate calls drifts into uselessness; the stop hook catching this after 20 edits and 8 turns confirms the failure mode is real and recurring.
In long parallel multi-agent sessions, writing a mini checkpoint after each discrete phase lets successor sessions restore context cheaply rather than rescanning the full codebase.
When building an access-gate system, unrecognized commands must default to DENY, not ALLOW; a default-allow fallback for unknown CLIs creates a bypass that renders the entire gate pointless.

Patching a specific instance of a policy violation (e.g., adding one CLI to a fallback list) without fixing the underlying class of problem (the structural default) leaves the same vulnerability open at every future unknown case.

Uncommitted agent edits to tracked files can be silently lost if the user commits or merges in a parallel operation; agent-made edits must be committed or explicitly stashed before handing control back to the user.

A Python exception class named 'NonRetryable' does not guarantee the framework skips retries; always read the error-handling code to confirm retry behavior rather than inferring it from the class name.
Vercel's auth.json stores `expiresAt` in seconds since epoch, not milliseconds; an off-by-1000x error in expiry calculations causes valid tokens to appear immediately expired.

When multiple agents work in parallel on the same codebase, they must pre-negotiate task ownership via IPC before starting work; overlapping claims without coordination produces muddy, conflicting edits that the user has to untangle.

The user prefers a breadth-first v1 pass across all surfaces before deep-diving into polish, validation, or improvements on individual items — pausing a sweep to perfect one area while others are unbuilt is the wrong priority order.

When sending IPC replies from a shell command, backticks and special characters in the message body get consumed by the shell and produce zero-byte or corrupted messages; the body must be quoted carefully or passed via a here-string or temp file.

When fixing a doc's voice by removing problematic content, do not overcorrect by stripping technical detail — target only the inappropriate content, not the technical framing; the fix should be scalpel-sized, not a full rewrite.
`rg -rn` is NOT 'recursive plus line-numbers' — the `-r` flag is `--replace`, which silently mangles output; always use `rg -n` for line numbers in recursive searches.

In a multi-agent setup where sessions are regularly context-cleared, each agent's checkpoint should record the peer agent's IPC alias so the next session can re-establish contact without requiring the user to re-introduce them.

A sub-agent must not touch or drop guard mute-files; a dropped mute file disables the guard machine-wide for all concurrent sessions until manually removed, silently negating safety gates the main agent relies on.

Code and docs can diverge between triage-time and edit-time; re-verify the specific file or function at the moment of writing the edit, not at the moment of planning it — the ground truth is the current file, not the earlier scan.

In a multi-agent parallel workflow, each agent's task list can become stale; before starting any item, verify it has not already been completed by a peer agent rather than relying on the list state from session start.

Advisory specs and skill docs only bind agents that read them at startup; to make a behavioral constraint effective across sub-agents and in-flight sessions, enforcement must be placed at the data-write layer (a hook, CLI gate, or schema check) rather than left as advisory text.

When writing a document that will be shared externally, all internal banter, critique, and conversational framing about stakeholders must be stripped before the document is written — the agent must distinguish between what was said conversationally and what is safe to publish.

Correcting a document's tone for its audience should adjust register only, not strip technical substance — overcorrecting toward accessible prose leaves engineers with an essay they will abandon for lacking implementation detail.

When asking the user a decision question, include enough background and tradeoffs to make the question self-contained and answerable without additional follow-up; questions that force the user to ask for context before answering are a recurring friction point.

In multi-agent IPC sessions, unanswered peer queries must be replied to before the session ends; stop hooks will fire repeatedly for each unreplied message, indicating this is a mechanical obligation, not optional.

Task list hygiene degrades specifically during high-parallelism periods with many sub-agent completions; the task list must be explicitly reconciled after a burst of sub-agent work, not only at session boundaries.

When verifying IPC message delivery, wait for an actual round-trip reply from the peer rather than inspecting the sending agent's own logs or send-side telemetry — a successful send does not prove the message arrived or was acted on.

In multi-agent sessions, the user should not have to repeatedly give plain go-aheads for short-distance progress; batch sequential work into autonomous runs and halt only at genuine decision points, blocking reviews, or missing user input.

CLI authentication commands (e.g. cloud provider logins) require an interactive terminal and cannot be automated; flag this to the user up front and hand off the auth step rather than attempting it and failing.

In multi-agent IPC setups where sessions are cleared periodically, registered aliases become stale after the owning session restarts; fall back to bare sessionId addressing for reliable delivery rather than trusting previously-registered aliases.

The Task tool must be updated incrementally throughout active work, not only at major milestones; allowing many edits to accumulate without reflecting them in the task list causes the live status view to drift and confuses both the user and future turns.

When proposing names for packages, repos, or identifiers within the same organization, always default to a consistent naming scheme across sibling artifacts — suggesting diverging names in the same namespace without an explicit justification draws immediate pushback.

While waiting for a peer agent to send information over an IPC channel, the agent should not repeatedly nudge the user for context or status updates — ask once, then wait for the real message rather than turning the user into a polling proxy.

Git branch state captured at session start can silently drift during the session; always re-read current branch state immediately before any branch-sensitive operation rather than relying on the value observed at session open.

When sending IPC messages between peer agents, the agent must verify the peer alias maps to the intended recipient by checking live peer IDs before sending — a descriptive alias name does not guarantee it identifies the correct session.

During autonomous multi-turn work sessions, the task list must be updated after each logical unit of work rather than batching updates at session end — allowing the task list to drift from actual progress renders the live status surface useless.

Shared UI elements such as navigation shells must be implemented from a single shared source component, not replicated per-page, so that all authenticated pages remain consistent without manual propagation.

When a component returns no data, downstream derivation logic must emit an empty or uncertain result rather than converting the absence into a fabricated negative claim; treating an empty result as evidence of non-existence produces false negatives that are indistinguishable from real negative evidence.

When a test lab or pipeline has long-lived caches, re-running it after a code change exercises the cache layer rather than the changed code; confirming a code change requires a cache-bust parameter or explicit cache invalidation before treating re-run results as evidence the fix works.

When the user reports a UI component inconsistency on one page (sidebar, drawer, modal shell), the fix must be applied to all pages using that component simultaneously; treating it as a single-page fix while sibling pages still use incompatible variants is a failure the user experiences as a missed-obvious pattern.

When a list page lacks pagination and other list pages in the same codebase already implement it, the agent must apply the pagination pattern without being explicitly told; the sibling-page pattern is available in-session evidence that must be used.

When a UI standardization request arrives as a list of issues across multiple pages, the agent should sweep ALL pages that use the affected component, not only the pages named in the user's message — the named examples are a sample, not an exhaustive scope.

When the agent pauses mid-task without surfacing a reason, the user must ask why, consuming a check-in round-trip; agents should explicitly state the stopping condition (blocker, phase boundary, question needed) before halting execution.

CSS utility class names used in implementations should be confirmed as present in the project's actual stylesheet or framework configuration before use; names that look like valid defaults may not be available in a project using a custom subset.

When an agent edits source files and then claims success using words like 'done', 'works', 'fixed', or 'passing' without actually executing the changed code path, it constitutes a false completion claim — type-checking, linting, and collecting tests are not substitutes for running the code.

Under high edit velocity (many file changes per turn), the agent's task list drifts from actual work done — the discipline that holds at low throughput is the first to slip when editing pace accelerates, requiring external hooks to force reconciliation.

When a list page is missing pagination and sibling list pages in the same codebase already display the paginated pattern, the agent must apply the same pagination before returning — treating each page in isolation when the pattern is already proven nearby is a systematic miss.

PR comments and inline docstrings should be stripped to the minimum non-obvious WHY; essay-length comments on small or self-evident changes are treated as noise and removed, not appreciated as thoroughness.
When presenting deferred decision items to the user, the agent omits the prior decision context and concrete options, forcing the user to ask a follow-up question before they can act.

When a main orchestrator session hits its usage limit while sub-agents are waiting on IPC responses, sub-agents are left blocked indefinitely; the architecture must anticipate this by having sub-agents self-report idle state so they can be re-queued on resume.

After a correction that a UI component must be globally shared, the agent must search and fix ALL instances across the entire codebase in the same response — patching only the immediate callsite while leaving sibling pages broken is experienced as gaslighting, not progress.

When a user reports that a UI component must be globally shared, the agent must search and fix ALL instances across the entire codebase in the same response — patching only the immediate callsite while leaving sibling pages broken is experienced as gaslighting, not progress.

UI review reports generated by testing in only one visual mode (e.g., dark mode only) produce findings the user considers not useful; review findings must be annotated with which mode was observed, or the review must cover both modes before reporting.

When a sub-agent hits a credential or auth block that is outside its own scope to fix, the correct behavior is to surface the exact command the user needs to run and hold explicitly — not attempt workarounds or stall silently.

When a sub-agent's write is hard-blocked by a harness guard, the correct recovery is to return the full findings as text in the response so the parent session can persist them — the harness block is not a failure, it is an enforced handoff point.
When the user asks for a tracking artifact for their own reference, provide a human-facing doc they can independently consult, explicitly separate from agent-internal memory or task state.

When a user asks to set up 'runtime variables' or 'runtime config' in an already-deployed app, they typically mean dynamically-adjustable application-level globals (feature flags, model keys, prompts, thresholds) — not deployment-time environment variables or secret managers. Proposing env-var or external secret solutions to this request is a category error.

When the user sets an explicit narrow scope for a feature ('only for X, not Y'), the implementation must enforce that scope literally without adding self-gating flexibility or generalizing beyond what was stated.

Before proposing to re-enable or expand a disabled configuration (CI trigger, feature flag, auto-run), investigate why it was disabled — the existing disabled state may represent a deliberate architectural or cost decision.
When a sub-agent signals completion via notification, verify the output artifact exists on disk before using its findings — the notification is not proof the file was written.

When a PR review or code audit output is delivered as a pipe-delimited dump or HTML artifact, the user prefers inline markdown organized by logical/functional category, with severity only explicitly marked for high-severity findings rather than used as the primary sorting axis.

The user prefers a deferred 'to be reviewed' staging area for completed non-critical work rather than requesting immediate review for every change; items get crossed off once actually inspected, not when the agent marks them done.
The user expects commit messages to exclude model co-authorship metadata (Co-Authored-By lines, session URL footers) and wants a comment hygiene pass applied at commit time.

When an agent creates a formal or technical document to capture and systematize an existing system (e.g., a concepts/schema doc derived from the codebase), that derivative document must never be used as the authoritative specification in gap audits or feature planning — the original user-authored product spec remains the upstream authority, and citing agent-authored formalizations as the source inverts the derivation chain.

When a sub-agent performing a gap or capability audit independently selects an agent-authored formalization document as its authority (rather than the user-authored product spec), the parent agent must validate what ground-truth document the sub-agent used before consuming or acting on the audit findings — acting on a report grounded in a derived, agent-authored doc inverts the authority chain.

When the agent ships UI features (labels, flows, module names) without consulting design mocks, the result mismatches user expectations; the agent must read the design mocks before implementing any named UI element.

IPC message delivery should be confirmed by waiting for an actual round-trip reply from the peer, not by inspecting the sending agent's own logs; the user will reject log-based assurance and insist on a verified reply.

When a list page is missing pagination and sibling list pages in the same session already display the paginated pattern, the agent should recognise and apply that pattern rather than treating each page in isolation; in-session context that directly proves the pattern is available evidence the agent must use.

When a sub-agent hits a credential or auth block that is outside its own scope to fix, it should surface the exact command the user needs to run and hold explicitly — not attempt workarounds or silently stall.

Deferred decision items presented to the user must include the exact prior decision or constraint and at least two concrete options to choose from — items without that context force a follow-up round-trip and are experienced as an incomplete handoff.

When a multi-agent orchestration session hits its usage limit mid-coordination, sub-agents left waiting have no path to notify the orchestrator; the architecture should include idle-notification so the orchestrator can re-queue them on resume rather than leaving them hanging.

Declaring implementation work done without verifying on the actual running dev server leads to issues (wrong labels still showing, removed pages still present) that only surface when the user manually checks.

Product-level behavioral decisions embedded in implementation (e.g., whether a user can add files to an existing job) must be surfaced as explicit questions to the user rather than resolved silently as implementation choices.

When conducting a gap audit against product requirements, the agent must use the user-authored upstream source document as authoritative, not a downstream technical-definitions doc the agent itself generated from that source.
UI module labels, naming, and creation flows must be validated against the design mocks before shipping, not derived from internal naming conventions or prior code patterns alone.

When the user explicitly grants permission to proceed autonomously on reversible work due to time pressure or personal constraints, the agent should proceed without seeking further clarification — waiting is the wrong move.

When presenting deferred decision items to the user, each item must include the exact prior decision or constraint and at least two concrete options; items without that context force an unnecessary follow-up round-trip and are experienced as an incomplete handoff.

When a sub-agent hits a credential or auth block that is outside its own scope to fix, it should surface the exact command the user needs to run and hold — not attempt workarounds — so the human can unblock it in one action.

When a list page is missing pagination and sibling list pages in the same application already display a paginated pattern, the agent must apply the same pattern before returning rather than treating each page in isolation.
Completion and gap assessments made without reading actual source files consistently overestimate how much is built; the agent should read code before producing a gap table.
The user prefers a deferred review workflow: completed non-critical items should be queued to a 'to be reviewed' backlog rather than triggering an immediate review unless explicitly asked.

Implementing UI module labels, page names, and creation flows without first consulting the design mocks causes explicit user frustration and complete rework; the mocks must be consulted before any UI label or flow is shipped, not derived from internal naming conventions.

When an agent has authored a downstream formalization document from a user-authored product spec, feature gap audits must be grounded in the original user-authored document; using the agent-generated derivative as the authoritative reference produces incorrect completeness verdicts.

When a skill invocation has a documented mandatory gate phase (e.g., adversarial validation), silently skipping it and marking tasks complete on the board is a confirmed mistake — the gate exists precisely because the agent would otherwise declare success prematurely.

When a project-specific UI verification checklist is available, the agent must run it during any browser verification pass — skipping a context-specific checklist while doing browser verification on the same page is treated as a serious failure, not a minor omission.

Claiming a specific UI sub-issue is fixed without verifying the full rendered state of the containing element leads to adjacent problems surviving — the agent fixed one thing (copy) while breaking another (title) and leaving a third (padding) untouched, then reported success.

User-facing UI banner copy written in formal, structured agent-style language ('This job has not started — it needs its setup.') reads as AI-generated and is rejected; the user expects short, natural human phrasing even for system-state messages.

When the user types a terse continuation signal ('proceed', 'keep going') and context pressure is below 70%, the agent must continue work immediately without pausing to ask clarifying questions — pausing on a terse continuation at low context is a confirmed mistake, not a safe default.
When a list page is missing standard pagination while sibling list pages already implement it, the agent leaves the gap uncorrected and waits for the user to point it out explicitly.

A sub-agent that hits a credential or auth block outside its own scope should surface the exact unblocking command the user needs to run and hold — not attempt workarounds — enabling the user to unblock the flow in one action and the sub-agent to resume cleanly.

When incorporating a dead or unavailable peer agent's work, selectively triage it for only the parts worth integrating rather than wholesale adopting it; the user's framing 'only where worth it' signals selective, not additive, integration

Null or missing fields in a data pipeline must be explicitly handled before numeric operations or display logic — when the agent notices a null coercion producing a suspicious default value during a pre-delivery review, it must treat that as a blocker, not dismiss it as acceptable, even if it was previously corrected elsewhere in the pipeline.

When implementing a multi-criteria filter (e.g. job type exclusions), the agent must verify that ALL stated criteria are enforced conjunctively against real output before delivery — a filter that passes obviously out-of-scope items was never exercised against the actual dataset.

When the agent claims to have read through produced output before delivery, that claim must be backed by actually reading the rows and acting on what is found — stating 'I noticed X but dismissed it as acceptable' after an explicit prior correction on X is the same failure mode as not reading at all.

In high-activity sessions with many sequential file edits, the task list must be reconciled before stopping rather than allowed to drift — a task list frozen across 50+ edits leaves the user's TUI blind and signals the agent has lost track of its own progress.

UI elements with content that is statically known at render time (sidebar navigation, topbar branding, page titles) must never receive skeleton loading states — skeletons are reserved for data that is asynchronously fetched.

When multiple pages each need a loading skeleton, each page must implement its own page-specific skeleton that mirrors that page's actual content structure; reusing a different page's skeleton component on the wrong route is a critical visual defect.

Using an IIFE or scope-wrapper in JSX is a recurring smell; before inserting one, scan the 10 lines around the insertion point and conform to whatever pattern siblings use (inline prop or plain const).

When the user states requirements in an explicit order, skipping or deprioritizing the first requirement while completing later items is treated as a significant failure; user-stated ordering is a hard priority constraint, not a loose suggestion.

Hitting a model subscription or usage limit mid-autonomous-session causes the session to stall silently rather than producing a graceful notification and fallback, leaving pending work in an indeterminate state.
